newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Mediator holds Bangui army reconciliation meeting.
newsitem.headline: Mediator holds Bangui army reconciliation meeting.

text.p: Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure brought together Central African Republic's rival army factions on Wednesday for a reconciliation ceremony to end political and ethnic bloodshed.

Supporters and opponents of President Ange-Felix Patasse attended the foreign ministry ceremony as part of efforts to set a January 25 peace accord back on track after bloody clashes in June between army dissidents and African peacekeepers.
"From this ceremony on, I would like there to be no former mutineers and no loyalists," Toumani Toure told the rivals.
"Only the people of Central African Republic, through a desire to achieve reconciliation, can help us to help them to resolve this problem."
Toumani Toure was the architect of the January 25 Bangui Accords, which ended three army mutinies in under a year.
A second ceremony is planned for Thursday to mark the reintegration of the dissident soldiers and their weapons into their respective units.
The mutinies began over pay and conditions but turned into a bid to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. They degenerated in ethnic killings.
Clashes between peacekeepers and army dissidents who had not rejoined their units under the January deal broke out on June 20. They lasted for a week.
The Red Cross says at least 100 people died in the clashes and an estimated 60,000 civilians fled the capital. Some have since returned home.
Under the latest deal Toumani Toure and Jean-Marc Simon, the ambassador of France, the former colonial power, undertook to guarantee the dissidents' security.
France intervened in January to halt fighting and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
Most of the mutineers were from the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.

General Francois Bozize, head of the Central African armed forces, attended Wednesday's ceremony along with one of his deputies, Colonel Auguste Gamba, who is close to the dissidents, plus Captain Anicet Saulet, their leader.
